source_text: Harum uanitatum aput Romanos auctor et constitutor Sabinus ille rex fuit, qui maxime animos hominum rudes atque inperitos nouis superstitionibus implicauit: quod ut faceret aliqua cum auctoritate, simulauit cum dea Egeria nocturnos se habere congressus. erat spelunca quaedam peropaca in nemore Aricino, unde riuus perenni fonte manabat. huc se remotis arbitris inferre consueuerat, ut mentiri posset monitu deae coniugis ea sacra populo se tradere, quae acceptissima diis essent. uidelicet astutiam Minois uoluit imitari, qui se in antrum Iouis recondebat et ibi diu moratus leges tamquam sibi a Ioue traditas adferebat, ut homines ad parendum non modo imperio, sed etiam religione constringeret. nec difficile sane fuit persuadere pastoribus. itaque pontifices flamines Salios augures creauit, deos per familias discripsit: sic noui populi feroces animos mitigauit et ad studia pacis a rebus bellicis auocauit. sed cum alios falleret, se ipsum tamen non fefellit. nam post annos plurimos Cornelio et Baebio consulibus in agro scribae Petili sub Ianiculo arcae duae lapideae sunt repertae a fossoribus, quarum in altera corpus Numae fuit, in altera septem Latini libri de iure pontificio, item Graeci totidem de disciplina sapientiae scripti, quibus religiones non eas modo quas ipse instituerat, sed omnes praeterea dissoluit. qua re ad senatum delata decretum est, ut hi libri abolerentur. ita eos Quintus Petilius praetor urbanus in contione populi concremauit. insipienter id quidem: quid enim profuit libros esse combustos, cum hoc ipsum, quod sunt ideo combusti, quia religionibus derogabant, memoriae sit traditum? nemo ergo tunc in senatu non stultissimus: potuerunt enim et libri aboleri et tamen res in memoriam non exire. ita dum uolunt etiam posteris adprobare quanta pietate defenderint religiones, auctoritatem religionum ipsarum testando minuerunt. sed ut Pompilius aput Romanos institutor ineptarum religionum fuit, sic ante Pompilium Faunus in Latio, qui et Saturno auo nefaria sacra constituit et Picum patrem inter deos honorauit et sororem suam Fentam Faunam eandemque coniugem consecrauit; quam Gauius Bassus tradit Fatuam nominatam, quod mulieribus fata canere consuesset ut Faunus uiris. eandem Varro scribit tantae pudicitiae fuisse, ut nemo illam quoad uixerit praeter suum uirum mas uiderit nec nomen eius audierit. idcirco illi mulieres in operto sacrificant et Bonam Deam nominant. et Sextus Clodius in eo libro quem Graece scripsit, refert Fauni hanc uxorem fuisse; quae quia contra morem decusque regium clam uini ollam ebiberat et ebria facta erat, uirgis myrteis a uiro ad mortem usque caesam; postea uero cum eum facti sui paeniteret ac desiderium eius ferre non posset, diuinum illi honorem detulisse; idcirco in sacris eius obuolutam uini amphoram poni. reliquit ergo posteris Faunus quoque non parum erroris, quem tamen prudentes quique perspiciunt. nam Lucilius eorum stultitiam, qui simulacra deos putant esse, deridet his uersibus: terriculas Lamias, Fauni quas Pompiliique instituere Numae, tremit has, hic omnia ponit. ut pueri infantes credunt signa omnia aena uiuere et esse homines, sic isti omnia ficta uera putant, credunt signis cor inesse in aenis. pergula pictorum, ueri nihil, omnia ficta! poeta quidem stultos homines infantibus conparauit, at ego multo inprudentiores esse dico. illi enim simulacra homines putant esse, hi deos; illos aetas facit putare quod non est, hos stultitia; illi utique breui desinent falli, horum uanitas et durat. semper et crescit. sacra Liberi patris primus Orpheus induxit in Graecia primusque celebrauit in monte Boeotiae Thebis ubi Liber natus est proximo; qui cum frequenter citharae cantu personaret, Cithaeron appellatus est. ea sacra etiamnunc Orphica nominantur, in quibus ipse postea dilaceratus et carptas est; et fuit per eadem fere tempora quibus Faunus. sed quis aetate praecesserit dubitari potest, siquidem per eosdem annos Latinus Priamusque regnarunt, item patres eorum Faunus et Laomedon, quo regnante Orpheus cum Argonautis ad Iliensium litus accessit. procedamus igitur ulterius et quaeramus, quis omnino colendorum deorum primus auctor extiterit. Didymus m libris ἐξηγήσεως Πινδαριϰη̆ς ait Melissea Cretensium regem primum diis sacrificasse ac ritus nouos sacrorumque pompas introduxisse; huius duas fuisse filias, Amaltheam et Melissam, quae Iouem puerum caprino lacte ac melle nutrierint — unde poetica illa fabula originem sumpsit apes aduolasse atque os pueri melle complesse —; Melissam uero a patre primam sacerdotem Matri Magnae constitutam, unde adhuc eiusdem Matris antistites Melissae nuncupentur. Historia uero Sacra testatur ipsum Iouem postquam rerum potitus sit, in tantam uenisse insolentiam, ut ipse sibi fana in multis locis constituerit. nam cum terras circumiret, ut in quamque regionem uenerat, reges principesue populorum hospitio sibi et amicitia copulabat et cum a quoque digrederetur, iubebat sibi fanum creari hospitis sui nomine, quasi ut posset amicitiae ac foederis memoria conseruari. sic constituta sunt templa Ioui Ataburio, Ioui Labryandio: Ataburus enim et Labryandus hospites eius atque adiutores in bello fuerunt; item Ioui Laprio, Ioui Molioni, Ioui Casio et quae sunt in eundem modum. quod ille astutissime excogitauit, ut et sibi honorem diuinum et hospitibus suis perpetuum nomen adquireret cum religione coniunctum. gaudebant ergo illi et huic imperio eius libenter obsequebantur et nominis sui gratia ritus annuos et festa celebrabant. simile quiddam in Sicilia fecit Aeneas, cum conditae urbi Acestae hospitis nomen inposuit, ut eam postmodum laetus ac libens Acestes diligeret augeret ornaret. hoc modo religionem cultus sui per orbem terrae Iuppiter seminauit et exemplum ceteris ad imitandum dedit. siue igitur a Melisseo, sicut Didymus tradidit, colendorum deorum ritus effluxit siue ab ipso Ioue, ut Euhemerus, de tempore tamen constat quando dii coli coeperint. Melisseus quidem multum antecessit aetate, quippe qui educauerit Iouem pro nepote. et idcirco fieri potest ut uel ante uel adhuc puero Ioue deos colere instituerit id est alumni sui matrem (Opem) et auiam Tellurem, quae fuit Urani coniunx, patremque Saturnum et ipse hoc exemplo atque instituto Iouem ad tantam superbiam prouexerit, ut postea sibi diuinos honores auderet assumere.
pass_a_gloss: Of these vanities among the Romans the author and founder was that King Sabinus, who most greatly entangled the rough and inexperienced minds of men with new superstitions: which so that he might do with some authority, he pretended that he had nocturnal meetings with the goddess Egeria. There was a certain very dark cave in the Arician forest, from which a stream flowed with a perpetual spring. Thither he was accustomed to go, having removed witnesses, so that he might be able to lie, on the advice of the goddess his wife, that he was handing over to the people those sacred rites which were most acceptable to the gods. Evidently he wished to imitate the cunning of Minos, who hid himself in a cave of Jupiter and, having stayed there for a long time, brought forth laws as if they had been handed over to him by Jupiter, so that he might constrain men to obey not only his command but also his religion. Nor was it indeed difficult to persuade shepherds. And so he created pontiffs, flamens, Salian priests, and augurs; he distributed the gods among families: thus he mitigated the fierce minds of the new people and turned them away from warlike things to the pursuits of peace. But while he was deceiving others, he did not nevertheless deceive himself. For after many years, in the consulship of Cornelius and Baebius, on the land of the scribe Petilius under the Janiculum, two stone chests were found by diggers, in one of which was the body of Numa, in the other seven Latin books on pontifical law, and as many Greek books on the discipline of wisdom, written in such a way that they dissolved not only the religions which he himself had instituted but all others besides. Which thing having been brought to the senate, it was decreed that these books should be destroyed. And so Quintus Petilius, the urban praetor, burned them in a public assembly of the people. Foolishly, indeed: for what did it profit that the books were burned, since this very thing, that they were burned because they derogated from religions, has been handed down to memory? Therefore no one then in the senate was not very foolish: for they were able to destroy the books and yet not bring the thing into memory. Thus, while they wish to approve to posterity how greatly they have defended religions with piety, they have diminished the authority of the religions themselves by testifying to them. But just as Pompilius was among the Romans the institutor of foolish religions, so before Pompilius, Faunus was in Latium, who established nefarious sacred rites for his grandfather Saturn and honored his father Picus among the gods and consecrated his sister and wife Fenta Fauna; whom Gaius Bassus hands down as being named Fata, because she was accustomed to sing fates to women, just as Faunus did to men. The same Varro writes that she was of such great chastity that no man except her husband saw her or heard her name while she lived. On this account, women sacrifice to her with covered heads and call her the Good Goddess. And Sextus Clodius, in that book which he wrote in Greek, reports that this wife of Faunus was; who, because she had drunk a jar of wine contrary to royal custom and decency, and had become drunk, was beaten to death with myrtle rods by her husband; afterwards, indeed, when he repented of his deed and was unable to bear the longing for her, he paid her divine honors; on this account, in her sacred rites, a jar of wine is placed, covered. Therefore Faunus also left to posterity not a little error, which, however, all prudent men perceive. For Lucilius derides the foolishness of those who think that statues are gods in these verses: 'The terriculas, the Lamias, which Faunus and Numa Pompilius instituted, he trembles at these, he places all things.' As infant children believe that all bronze statues are living and are men, so these men think that all fabricated things are true, they believe that there is a heart in the bronze statues. The stage of painters, nothing true, all fabricated! The poet, indeed, compared foolish men to infant children, but I say that they are much more imprudent. For they think that statues are gods, those think that they are men; their age makes them think what is not, foolishness makes these men think; those will certainly cease to be deceived soon, the vanity of these men, however, lasts and always grows. The sacred rites of Father Liber were first introduced into Greece by Orpheus and first celebrated on Mount Thebes in Boeotia, where Liber was born; who, since he often resounded with the song of the cithara, was called Cithaeron. These sacred rites are even now called Orphic, in which he himself was later torn apart and torn to pieces; and he lived at almost the same time as Faunus. But who preceded the other in age can be doubted, since Latinus and Priam reigned in the same years, as did their fathers, Faunus and Laomedon, during whose reign Orpheus came to the shore of the Ilians with the Argonauts. Let us proceed, therefore, and seek who was the first author of the worship of the gods. Didymus, in his books of the 'Exegesis of Pindar', says that Melisseus, the king of the Cretans, was the first to sacrifice to the gods and introduce new rites and pomp of sacred rites; that he had two daughters, Amalthea and Melissa, who nourished Jupiter as a boy with goat's milk and honey — whence that poetic fable took its origin, that bees flew to him and filled the mouth of the boy with honey —; that Melissa was indeed constituted by her father as the first priestess of the Great Mother, whence even now the priestesses of the same Mother are called Melissae. The Sacred History, however, testifies that Jupiter himself, after he had become powerful, came to such great insolence that he himself established temples for himself in many places. For when he was traveling through the lands, so that in whatever region he came, he bound the kings and princes of the peoples to himself with hospitality and friendship, and when he departed from each one, he ordered that a temple be built for himself in the name of his host, as if the memory of the friendship and pact might be preserved. Thus temples were established for Jupiter Ataburius, Jupiter Labrandius: for Ataburus and Labrandius were his hosts and helpers in war; similarly for Jupiter Laprius, Jupiter Molion, Jupiter Casius, and those which are in the same manner. Which thing he cleverly devised, so that he might acquire both divine honor for himself and perpetual name for his hosts, connected with religion. Therefore they rejoiced and willingly obeyed his command, and for the sake of his name, they celebrated annual rites and festivals. Aeneas did something similar in Sicily, when he founded the city of Acesta and gave it the name of his host, so that Acestes might later love, increase, and adorn it. In this way Jupiter sowed the seed of the worship of himself throughout the earth and gave an example to others to imitate. Whether, therefore, the rites of the worship of the gods flowed from Melisseus, as Didymus handed down, or from Jupiter himself, as Euhemerus, it is certain, however, from what time the gods began to be worshiped. Melisseus, indeed, preceded by a long time, since he educated Jupiter as if he were his grandson. And therefore it can be that he instituted the worship of the gods either before or while Jupiter was still a boy, that is, his foster child's mother (Opis) and grandmother Tellus, who was the wife of Uranus, and his father Saturn, and that Jupiter himself, following this example and institution, was driven to such great pride that afterwards he dared to assume divine honors for himself.
